families.s: HSE permit-to-work systems for major-hazard plant
families.t: authorisation, hot work, vessel entry, isolation, draining, flushing, monitoring, handback and audit
f: Permit-to-work systems control hazardous maintenance and similar non-routine work.
Permits should identify the work, hazards, precautions, responsible persons and authorisation.
Permit types may include hot work, cold work, excavation, vessel entry and equipment removal.
Preparations can include isolation, draining, flushing and atmospheric monitoring.
Workers should understand the hazardous environment and the permit conditions.
Introducing ignition sources into classified areas requires explicit control.
Completed work should be formally handed back to operations in a safe condition.
Permit systems should be managed, recorded, inspected, reviewed and audited.
families.g: Authorisation, hot work, vessel entry, isolation, draining, flushing, monitoring, handback and audit guidance is general process-safety evidence and does not prove current controls, condition, inventory, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.t: separation, site boundaries, domino effects, occupied buildings, confinement, emergency access, escape and maintainability
f: Plant layout balances transfer distances, site constraints, operations and safety.
Hazardous-material facilities should be located with regard to site boundaries and neighbouring populations.
Layout should avoid confinement where flammable releases may occur.
Separation can prevent or reduce escalation and domino effects.
Occupied buildings should be located and protected for credible major-hazard events.
Emergency services need suitable access to plant areas.
Personnel need effective emergency escape routes.
Layout should support safe operation, inspection, maintenance and control of unauthorised access.
families.g: Separation, site boundaries, domino effects, occupied buildings, confinement, emergency access, escape and maintainability guidance is general process-safety evidence and does not prove current controls, condition, inventory, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.s: HSE plant modification and management-of-change procedures
families.t: plant, procedures, people, substances, risk assessment, authorisation, documentation, training and pre-startup review
f: Formal management procedures should cover changes to plant, equipment, procedures, people and substances.
Proposed changes should be risk assessed before implementation.
Assessments should consider the possibility and consequences of hazards being realised.
Previous incidents and the validity of existing hazard studies should inform the review.
Preventive and protective measures may need redesign when the process definition changes.
Changes should be authorised, documented and communicated to affected personnel.
Drawings, procedures, training and maintenance information should be updated.
A pre-startup or return-to-service check should confirm that approved safeguards are in place.

families.s: HSE quench systems for runaway reactions and emergency vent streams
families.t: cooling, dilution, reaction control, dump tanks, vent treatment, solvent mixing, design, reliability and testing
f: Quenching can directly control a chemical reaction or treat an emergency vent stream.
A direct quench cools and dilutes reactants to reduce reaction and heat-generation rates.
Quench material may be added to the reactor.
Reactants may instead be discharged to a dedicated dump tank.
Vent-stream quenching can condense volatile components and cool continuing reactions.
Quench chemistry and quantity should be compatible with the credible runaway scenario.
Delivery systems should act quickly enough and remain available when demanded.
Quench systems require suitable design, maintenance, testing and integration with relief and containment.

families.s: HSE raw-material control and process sampling
families.t: identity, contamination, specification, delivery acceptance, sampling, quality assurance, compatibility and traceability
f: Raw-material control should prevent the wrong or contaminated chemical entering a process.
The approach applies from receipt through use and disposal.
A chemical may be a contaminant, raw material, reactant, intermediate, by-product or product.
Controls should consider the consequences of using the wrong material in the wrong place.
Out-of-specification or contaminated material can initiate dangerous reactions or attack plant.
Delivery acceptance, sampling and quality-control tasks require competent procedures.
Identity, specification and compatibility should be confirmed before material is introduced.
Records and traceability should support investigation and control throughout the material lifecycle.
